summary: Describes a URN namespace that the Open Grid Forum created for naming persistent resources. URNs give lasting names that do not depend on where something is stored. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A URN is like a name that stays with you even if you move house. This sets up a name category for a grid computing group to name its stuff.

subtitle: Persistent identifiers for grid computing resources and standards

tldr.problem: The Open Grid Forum works on standards and resources for distributed computing but lacked a way to assign persistent, globally unique names to those resources that would not change if documents moved or were reorganized.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers the "ogf" URN namespace with IANA, allowing the OGF to assign URNs in the form urn:ogf:subnamespace:resource-id and delegate parts of the namespace to other organizations or communities.
tldr.outcome: The OGF has a formal mechanism to name grid standards, documents, and resources with persistent identifiers that remain valid regardless of where resources are stored.

today: RFC 6453 remains in effect as the formal definition of the OGF URN namespace. The OGF maintains the registry at ogf.org/urn/ where subnamespace identifiers and their documentation are published. The namespace has been successfully assigned to the OGF and enables persistent naming of grid computing resources and standards.

sections.title: URNs for the Open Grid Forum
sections.content:
The Open Grid Forum (OGF) is a standards organization focused on distributed computing. The OGF produces many technical documents including working drafts, specifications, and XML and RDF schemas that members of the distributed computing community reference.

Unlike URLs (Uniform Resource Locators) that describe where something is stored on a network, a URN (Uniform Resource Name) provides a permanent identifier that does not depend on location. OGF working groups expressed a need for such global, persistent identifiers for their resources. This RFC formalizes that need by registering an OGF namespace with IANA, allowing the OGF to assign URNs to its documents and schemas.
sections.plainLanguage: Grid computing is a field where many computers work together. The OGF makes standards for that field. They wanted permanent names for those standards that would not change if moved to a different location.

sections.title: How OGF URNs are Structured
sections.content:
All OGF URNs follow the pattern urn:ogf:SNID:SUBNAMESPACE-SPECIFIC-STRING, where ogf is the namespace identifier registered with IANA.

The SNID (subnamespace identifier) is a unique code assigned by the OGF Technical Director to identify a particular category of resources. The SNID uses the same character set as a standard URN namespace identifier: alphanumerics and hyphens, up to 32 characters long. For example, the OGF might assign "gfd" as a subnamespace for Grid Forum Documents, and "network" for network-related resources.

The SUBNAMESPACE-SPECIFIC-STRING is the unique identifier within that subnamespace, and its syntax depends on the rules defined for that particular SNID. The OGF Technical Director maintains a registry at ogf.org/urn/ of all assigned subnamespace identifiers and their documentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it as a nested naming system: the top level is "ogf," then each category (like documents or networks) gets its own letter code, and then individual items get unique names within that category.

sections.title: Assigning and Managing Subnamespaces
sections.content:
The OGF Technical Director is responsible for assigning new subnamespace identifiers (SNIDs). Before a SNID can be assigned, the OGF must publish a Grid Forum Document that formally defines the syntax and semantics of that subnamespace. This ensures that the naming scheme for each category is well-documented and consistent.

The OGF may sub-delegate portions of its namespace to third parties or other organizations. Once a SNID is assigned, it may never be reassigned to a different purpose, ensuring that a URN assigned today will always refer to the same resource and will remain valid indefinitely.

The RFC notes that while the namespace is not currently registered with a Resolution Discovery System (RDS), nothing prevents such registration in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: The grid computing group carefully decides what names to create and writes down the rules for each category. Once a name is assigned, it is locked in forever so nothing ever loses its name.

sections.title: Persistence and Uniqueness Guarantees
sections.content:
The RFC enforces two critical guarantees. First, identifier uniqueness is guaranteed by the OGF Technical Director, who will not permit duplicate SNIDs and will not allow a previously assigned subnamespace to be reassigned unless special arrangements are made to prevent conflicts.

Second, identifier persistence is guaranteed through formal requirements: the OGF will only assign SNIDs for persistent resources, and each subnamespace document must specify what type of resource it names (whether a specific version, the latest version, a general concept, or a particular manifestation). Most importantly, the RFC requires that the "ogf" namespace identifier itself must never change, even if the Open Grid Forum changes its name or is disbanded.
sections.plainLanguage: Once something gets a name, that name is locked down forever. No two things get the same name. And even if the OGF changes, the names stay the same.

sections.title: Validation and Security
sections.content:
URNs in the OGF namespace have no special security considerations beyond those that apply to URNs in general. However, each subnamespace SHOULD define its own validation mechanism to determine whether a URN is correctly formed according to that subnamespace's rules.

The RFC recommends that URN subnamespaces forbid certain special characters (%, /, ?, #) in the subnamespace-specific string to avoid ambiguity with URI syntax. For forward compatibility, software implementations should validate OGF URNs according to generic URI validation rules if they do not implement subnamespace-specific validation.

The RFC also recommends that implementers check the OGF registry and documentation before assuming a given identifier is valid, since the meaning and registration status of an identifier is determined by what the OGF publishes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each category of names gets its own rules for what makes a valid name. And you should check the official list to make sure a name is real before trusting it.
